finding.title: ThinVec::clear double-frees elements when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: clear() is safe public API that runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` (line 1084) and only afterwards resets the length via `self.set_len(0)` (line 1085). If any element's Drop panics (e.g. ThinVec<Box<_>>/ThinVec<String> where a user Drop impl panics), the panic unwinds before set_len(0), so the ThinVec's stored length still covers the elements whose destructors already ran. During unwinding the value is dropped again and ThinVec::drop calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` (line 1917) over that stale length, re-running Drop on and re-freeing already-freed heap objects (double free / use-after-free, RUSTSEC-2026-0103 / CVE-2026-6654). std's Vec::clear avoids this by setting len to 0 before dropping; thin-vec 0.2.15 does not, and patched versions are >= 0.2.16. Reachable using only safe code: push heap-owning elements whose Drop can panic, call v.clear() (optionally inside catch_unwind), and let v drop.

finding.title: IntoIter::drop double-frees remaining elements if an element Drop panics
finding.evidence: IntoIter::drop's drop_non_singleton moves the backing ThinVec into a local via `mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())` (line 2546) and then sequentially destroys the remaining elements with `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (line 2547) before resetting the length with `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (line 2548). If any element's Drop panics, the unwind skips the length reset, and the local `vec` is then dropped by the ThinVec Drop impl, which calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` (line 1917) over the unchanged length, re-dropping and re-freeing already-freed elements (double free / use-after-free, RUSTSEC-2026-0103 / CVE-2026-6654). std::vec::IntoIter prevents this with a DropGuard; thin-vec 0.2.15 lacks one (patched >= 0.2.16). Reachable from safe code by taking v.into_iter(), consuming some elements, and dropping the iterator when a remaining element's Drop panics.

finding.title: Chunked decoder discards any 2 bytes as the chunk footer without validating CRLF, enabling HTTP request/response smuggling
finding.evidence:
ChunkedReader.__call__ blindly consumes and throws away two bytes after each complete chunk: line 197 sets `self._bytes_to_discard = 2` (a bare count, not the expected `
`), and on the following call line 164 executes `data = buf.maybe_extract_at_most(self._bytes_to_discard)` followed by lines 167-169 which only decrement the counter, never comparing the consumed bytes to `
`. The bytes come directly from the remote peer's stream via ReceiveBuffer, so an attacker controls them. PoC against this tree (h11 0.14.0) with the request `POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: x
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

1
A!!0

` is ACCEPTED, yielding Request -> Data(b'A') -> EndOfMessage even though the chunk terminator `!!` is not CRLF; likewise `1
A

0

` (bare LF terminator) is accepted. Upstream h11 0.16.0 rejects both with `malformed chunk footer ... (expected b'
')` because it stores and compares the literal terminator (`self._bytes_to_discard = b"
"`). Because h11 silently tolerates malformed chunk boundaries while a front-end/proxy or a peer parser requires `
`, two HTTP parsers derive different message boundaries, i.e. request smuggling/desync (CVE-2025-43859). No other check in this file verifies the footer bytes.

finding.title: argon2i_32 uses unvalidated nb_blocks to size the Argon2 work area, causing a heap buffer overflow
finding.evidence: argon2i_32() takes nb_blocks from the caller and hard-codes nb_lanes=1 (line 330) but never enforces Monocypher's contract nb_blocks >= 8*nb_lanes before turning it into working-memory geometry: line 345 allocates work_area = malloc(nb_blocks * 1024) and line 347 immediately calls crypto_argon2(hash, ..., work_area, config, inputs, extras) on it. Inside monocypher.c:752-754 the real geometry is derived as segment_size = nb_blocks/nb_lanes/4, lane_size = segment_size*4, nb_blocks = lane_size*nb_lanes, which rounds down, so for nb_blocks == 0 malloc(0) returns a zero/minimal block yet monocypher.c:776-782 still writes two full 1024-byte blocks (blocks[0], blocks[1]) past it (heap buffer overflow write), and for 1 <= nb_blocks <= 7 lane_size collapses (0 for nb_blocks < 4) so monocypher.c:914 reads blocks[lane_size-1] == blocks[-1], leaking out-of-bounds heap memory into the returned hash. Reproduced against the shipped 4.0.2.6 build: monocypher.argon2i_32(0, 1, b'password', b'saltsaltsaltsalt') terminates the interpreter with SIGSEGV. The fix in 4.0.2.7 adds 'if config.nb_blocks < (config.nb_lanes * 8): raise ValueError(...)' immediately after the config assignments, confirming this is the missing precondition (GHSA-8f95-v3jq-cj86 / CVE-2026-53720).

finding.title: TOCTOU symlink following in UnixFileLock._acquire() truncates arbitrary files
finding.evidence: UnixFileLock._acquire() establishes the file-exists precondition with a separated check at lines 42-43 (open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC, then `if not Path(self.lock_file).exists(): open_flags |= os.O_CREAT`) and then opens the path at line 44 with os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode) without O_NOFOLLOW. A local attacker who can write to the directory holding the (predictable) lock file can, in the window between the Path.exists() check and the os.open() call, replace the lock path with a symlink to a victim file; the kernel follows the link and the O_TRUNC flag truncates the target, corrupting/destroying any file the locking process can write (the filelock advisory notes downstream victims such as virtualenv configs and PyTorch caches). No protection exists in this revision: O_NOFOLLOW is not added to open_flags, and the check-then-open gap is exactly the TOCTOU window. Upstream fixed this in 3.20.1 (CVE-2025-68146 / GHSA-w853-jp5j-5j7f) by adding O_NOFOLLOW.

finding.title: TOCTOU symlink/junction following in WindowsFileLock._acquire() truncates arbitrary files
finding.evidence: WindowsFileLock._acquire() builds flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_CREAT | os.O_TRUNC at lines 22-26 and then opens the lock path at line 28 with os.open(self.lock_file, flags, self._context.mode) without any reparse-point/symlink check (no GetFileAttributesW FILE_ATTRIBUTE_REPARSE_POINT verification). A local attacker able to write into the lock-file directory can pre-place or race in a symlink/junction at the predictable lock path between the directory/permission checks and the open; os.open() follows the reparse point and O_TRUNC truncates the victim file, corrupting arbitrary user files. This revision contains no mitigation (the O_NOFOLLOW-style defense and the reparse-point rejection are absent). Upstream fixed this in 3.20.1 (CVE-2025-68146 / GHSA-w853-jp5j-5j7f).

finding.title: TOCTOU symlink vulnerability between permission check and os.open() in SoftFileLock._acquire()
finding.evidence: SoftFileLock._acquire() first validates the path with raise_on_not_writable_file(self.lock_file) at line 17 (which itself os.stat()s the path, following symlinks, in filelock/_util.py line 22) and then opens it at line 27 with os.open(self.lock_file, flags, self._context.mode); the flags constructed at lines 20-25 (O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_TRUNC) do not include O_NOFOLLOW. Between the permission check and the open, a local attacker with write access to the lock directory can plant a symlink at the predictable lock path, so the lock operation resolves to an attacker-chosen target, enabling silent lock-acquisition failure, denial of service, and unintended file operations against the link target. The code adds no O_NOFOLLOW and performs no link resolution check, so the check-then-use gap is exploitable. Upstream fixed this in 3.20.3 (CVE-2026-22701 / GHSA-qmgc-5h2g-mvrw) by adding O_NOFOLLOW to the open flags.

finding.title: ThinVec::clear skips set_len(0) when an element's Drop panics, causing double free/UAF
finding.evidence: clear() first runs ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..]) (line 1084) and only afterwards resets the length via self.set_len(0) (line 1085). If any element's Drop implementation panics while the slice is being dropped, unwinding skips set_len(0), so the ThinVec still advertises its original length and still owns the elements whose destructors already ran and whose heap payloads were already freed. When the same container is later dropped (ThinVec::drop -> drop_non_singleton at line 1917 re-invokes ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])) or when catch_unwind lets scope exit proceed, the already-freed elements are dropped a second time, giving a double free and use-after-free. Reachability requires only safe code: put heap-owning values (Box/String) whose Drop can panic at a later index into a ThinVec, call v.clear(), and let unwinding proceed. std's Vec uses a DropGuard around this exact code to decrement len during unwinding; thin-vec 0.2.15 has no such guard (the guard was added in the 0.2.16 fix), so the precondition (len reset only after the fallible drop_in_place) is what enables the corruption.

finding.title: IntoIter::drop frees elements then skips set_len_non_singleton(0) on element-drop panic, double-freeing the buffer
finding.evidence: IntoIter::drop calls drop_non_singleton (line 2544), which takes ownership of the buffer with mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new()) (line 2546) and then performs ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..]) (line 2547); vec.set_len_non_singleton(0) (line 2548) only runs after that drop completes. If a remaining element's Drop panics, unwinding skips line 2548 and the local `vec` is itself dropped while still carrying its old length, so ThinVec::drop (line 1917) calls drop_in_place over every slot a second time: elements already freed in the loop are freed again (double free/UAF), and for a partially consumed iterator elements already yielded via next() have been moved out and dropped by the caller and are now freed again from the stale buffer. Safe-code trigger: build a ThinVec of heap-owning values where one later element panics in Drop, do `let mut it = v.into_iter(); it.next();` and drop the iterator (directly or via unwinding under catch_unwind). std::vec::IntoIter protects this with a drop guard; thin-vec 0.2.15 does not (the DropGuard around the len reset was added in the 0.2.16 fix).

finding.title: Double drop in ThinVec::clear when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: `clear()` unconditionally runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` on the whole slice at line 1084 and only afterwards resets the length via `self.set_len(0)` at line 1085. The length is never decremented before destruction, so if any element's `Drop::drop` panics (unwinds), line 1085 is skipped and the vector keeps its old length while the elements are already considered destroyed. The panic then unwinds out of the safe `clear()` call and `Drop for ThinVec` (line 1917, `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])`) destroys the very same elements a second time, i.e. a double drop / double free of `T`. This is reachable from entirely safe code (`ThinVec<T>::clear()` where `T: Drop` can panic). A local PoC with three elements whose `Drop` panics once reported 6 element drops instead of 3, and the second pass frees already-freed values. thin-vec 0.2.16 fixed exactly this by adding a DropGuard that sets len to 0 even on unwind.

finding.title: Double drop in IntoIter::drop when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: `IntoIter<T>::drop` calls `drop_non_singleton`, which at line 2546 moves the vector out with `mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())` into the local `vec` (the local therefore still carries the original, full length) and then calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` at line 2547. Only if no element panics does line 2548 (`vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)`) execute. If an element in `this.start..` panics while being dropped, the length is never zeroed, and unwinding drops the local `vec`, whose `Drop for ThinVec` (line 1917) runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` over the full original length: it re-drops the already-destroyed tail and also drops the already-moved-out head elements (`use`/`drop` of moved data). The result is a double free and use-after-free of `T`; in practice a second panic during unwinding aborts the process. This is triggered by safe code: dropping an `IntoIter` (or finishing iteration) when `T::Drop` panics. Fixed in thin-vec 0.2.16 by a DropGuard that zeroes the length on unwind; confirmed locally where dropping the iterator after `next()` caused repeated drops of the same elements and an abort.

finding.title: Missing lower bound on inBlockIndex lets prover force an all-zero SHA-256 output
finding.evidence: inBlockIndex is derived non-deterministically at line 110 (`inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9)`) and the only constraint on it is `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` (line 111); bitLengthVerifier (lines 125-128) only bounds the length from above. paddedInLength is a caller input (Sha256Bytes line 19, wired as `paddedInLength * 8` at line 33) and is never required to be >= 512, so a prover sets paddedInLength = 0, forcing inBlockIndex = 0. Line 195 then sets `arraySelectors[k].index = inBlockIndex - 1 = -1` (field element p-1). ItemAtIndex (array.circom lines 25-28) checks only `index < maxBlocks`; circomlib LessThan compares `index + 2^n - maxArrayLen` modulo the BN254 prime, so p-1 still satisfies `lessThan.out === 1`, and since no IsEqual(i, p-1) matches, calcTotal.sum = 0 and every out[k] = 0. A satisfying witness therefore exists for 'SHA256(paddedIn) = 0' with arbitrary paddedIn, breaking soundness (the identical defect is duplicated for Sha256Partial at lines 233-234 / 292).

finding.title: Sha256Partial/Sha256BytesPartial accept inBlockIndex = 0 and output zero hash
finding.evidence: In Sha256Partial the same unconstrained derivation is used: line 233 `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9)` with the sole constraint `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` at line 234, and the upper-only check bitLengthVerifier at lines 237-240. paddedInLength is fed from Sha256BytesPartial (line 65, `sha.paddedInLength <== paddedInLength * 8`, input declared line 50), so setting the byte length to 0 yields inBlockIndex = 0. Line 292 computes `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` = p-1, which ItemAtIndex accepts because its LessThan bound is defeated by field wraparound (array.circom lines 25-28), producing out[k] = 0 for all k. This lets a prover satisfy Sha256BytesPartial for the false statement 'hash(state, paddedIn) = 0' regardless of the chosen preHash and paddedIn.

finding.title: ItemAtIndex range check does not reject negative (p-1) index
finding.evidence: The only bound on index is `component lessThan = LessThan(bitLength)` with `lessThan.in[0] <== index` and `lessThan.in[1] <== maxArrayLen`, `lessThan.out === 1` (lines 25-28). circomlib's LessThan decomposes `in[0] + (1<<n) - in[1]` with Num2Bits, so the reduction is modulo the BN254 prime: with index = p-1 and bitLength = log2Ceil(maxArrayLen), the value becomes `d-1 = 2**bitLength - maxArrayLen - 1`, which is below 2**bitLength, so `out === 1` passes and no non-negativity check exists. Because every eqs[i] (lines 34-42) compares i in [0, maxArrayLen-1] against p-1, calcTotal.sum is 0, so ItemAtIndex silently returns 0 for the out-of-range index. Callers in sha.circom (arraySelectors with `index <== inBlockIndex - 1` at lines 195 and 292) rely on this check, so the underflow at inBlockIndex = 0 becomes a satisfied witness that forces the SHA-256 output to zero.

finding.title: Chunked-body chunk footer is discarded without verifying it is CRLF, enabling request smuggling
finding.evidence:
Peer bytes fed to Connection.receive_data() reach ChunkedReader.__call__ (h11/_readers.py:157). After each chunk of body data is consumed (line 195), line 197 sets self._bytes_to_discard = 2, i.e. it stores only a *count* of bytes rather than the expected terminator b"
"; lines 163-167 then extract and silently consume those 2 bytes (self._bytes_to_discard -= len(data)) with no comparison against b"
". The only framing validation in this reader is validate(chunk_header_re, chunk_header, ...) at lines 177-182, which constrains the chunk-size *header* line only, so any two bytes (including bare LFs or arbitrary garbage) are accepted as the chunk footer. Verified locally against this tree: h11 0.14.0 accepts b"POST / HTTP/1.1
...Transfer-Encoding: chunked

" + b"1
aXX0

" and + b"5
hello

0

" (returns Data + EndOfMessage), whereas the patched 0.16.0 raises "malformed chunk footer: bytearray(b'XX') (expected b'
')". Because a front-end proxy whose chunked decoder reads forward until a CRLF finds the footer (e.g. pound's historical bug) terminates/continues the same byte stream at a different offset than h11, an attacker can desynchronize request framing between the proxy and the h11-based server and smuggle a second request into the connection: CVE-2025-43859 / GHSA-vqfr-h8mv-ghfj (CVSS 3.1 9.1).

finding.title: Quote token can be added/moved into buckets priced at or above an active auction price, enabling auction manipulation
finding.evidence: addQuoteToken only calls _revertIfAuctionClearable (Pool.sol:158), which reverts solely when the head auction is already clearable (72h elapsed or no collateral left); an in-progress auction does not block deposits. LenderActions.addQuoteToken validates only index bounds (LenderActions.sol:158) and LUP/dust/fee (LenderActions.sol:175) and moveQuoteToken validates only indices/dust (LenderActions.sol:250-255); neither ever compares the target bucket price with the head auction price. An attacker (fully in control of amount_, index_, fromIndex_, toIndex_) can therefore inject or move quote into a bucket priced >= the live auction price, then arb-take (bucketTake) or otherwise steer the auction (value extraction from the pool / denial of take), which later releases explicitly suppress with a new _revertIfAuctionPriceBelow(auctions_, index_) guard that reverts AddAboveAuctionPrice ('prevents manipulative deposits and arbTakes').

finding.title: Claimable-Reserve-Auction can be kicked while borrower auctions are still active, consuming reserves committed to pending liquidations
finding.evidence: kickReserveAuction's only precondition is the timestamp guard at line 215 (2 weeks since last burn event and >72h since last CRA kick); there is no check on auctions_.noOfAuctions. Anyone can therefore start a reserve auction (claiming the 1% kickerAward at line 229 and locking the remainder as reserveAuction_.unclaimed at line 235) while borrower auctions are still unsettled. Because unclaimed is excluded from _availableQuoteToken() and _claimableReserves uses poolBalance/totalBondEscrowed, kicking a CRA at this point drains the reserves needed to cover the pending auctions' bonds/bad debt, causing losses for lenders/kickers. Later releases add _revertIfActiveAuctions(auctions_) (reverting AuctionActive when auctions_.noOfAuctions != 0) before starting a CRA.

finding.title: settlePoolDebt uses unlimited pool reserves to clear a single borrower's bad debt
finding.evidence: After the 72h permissionless-settle precondition at line 113, settlePoolDebt computes assets = poolState_.t0Debt - settled + borrower debt (in quote) + poolBalance (line 135) and liabilities = DEPOSIT_BUFFER*treeSum + totalBondEscrowed + reserveAuction.unclaimed (lines 137-141), then forgives the borrower's debt with the entire reserve excess via borrower.t0Debt -= Maths.min(borrower.t0Debt, assets - liabilities) (line 145) - there is no per-borrower cap. Any caller can settle one auction with collateral==0 and consume all claimable reserves, starving other pending liquidations and spending quote that is owed to lenders and escrowed bondholders. Later releases cap this with auctions_.liquidations[borrower].t0ReserveSettleAmount (= BorrowerT0Debt * borrowFeeRate / 2) and only during a 144h settlement window, confirming the unbounded reserve consumption here is the defect.
